scale.label: Scale

summary.trueScale: Real sizes, real distances. Space is almost entirely empty.
summary.trueScale@simple: Everything is as big and as far apart as in real life. Space is mostly empty!
summary.trueScale@advanced: True to scale: sizes and distances share one ruler. The planets fill almost none of the space between them.
summary.textbook: Like a textbook picture: real sizes, but the planets are pulled close together. Not to scale!
summary.textbook@simple: Like a picture in a school book: the planets are pulled close together. It is not really like this!
summary.textbook@advanced: Sizes true to each other, distances compressed: the picture most diagrams show. Not to scale.
summary.bigPlanets: Real distances, but the planets are drawn far too big – and they are still lost in empty space.
summary.bigPlanets@simple: The planets are made much bigger, but they are as far apart as in real life. They still look tiny!
summary.bigPlanets@advanced: Distances true, sizes exaggerated: even enlarged tenfold, the planets are specks along their orbits.
summary.everythingVisible: Made to show everything at once: the planets are drawn too big and too close together. Not to scale!
summary.everythingVisible@simple: The planets are made bigger and pulled closer, so you can see them all. It is not really like this!
summary.everythingVisible@advanced: Sizes exaggerated and distances compressed, so every body is visible at once. Not to scale.

spin.label: Spin

hint.realistic: Every planet turns at its true speed for the clock, so day and night match the date.
hint.realistic@simple: The planets spin exactly as fast as in real life.
hint.slowed: Spinning slowed down so that Earth turns at most once every {seconds, number} seconds. Orbits keep their speed; the other planets stay faster or slower than Earth.
hint.slowed@simple: The planets spin slower, so you can still see them turn when time runs fast. Earth takes at least {seconds, number} seconds for one turn.
hint.slow: Spinning slowed down so that Earth turns at most once every {seconds, number} seconds: slow enough to watch a single day pass. Orbits keep their speed.
hint.slow@simple: The planets spin very slowly, so you can watch one day go by. Earth takes at least {seconds, number} seconds for one turn.
hint.stopped: No planet spins, so the seasons are easy to follow as the planets travel round the Sun. Moons still keep one face toward their planet.
hint.stopped@simple: The planets stop spinning. They still travel round the Sun.

spin.notice: Not true to the clock: day and night on the planets no longer match the date.
spin.notice@simple: The planets spin slower than in real life.

birthday.openHint: How old are you on other planets?
birthday.title: Your birthday in space
birthday.intro: Pick the day you were born. You will see how old you are on every planet, where the planets stood that day and how far you have travelled.
birthday.intro@simple: When were you born? Pick the day and find out how old you are on the other planets!
birthday.intro@advanced: Pick a date of birth. Ages, days and weights are computed from each world’s orbital period, rotation and surface gravity.
birthday.calendarHint: First the year, then the month, then the day.
birthday.privacy: Nothing is saved or sent anywhere. Your birthday stays on this screen and is forgotten when you close the page.
birthday.privacy@simple: Your birthday is not saved and not sent anywhere. When you close the page, it is gone.
birthday.privacyLink: While a birthday is entered, links to this page leave out the date.
birthday.showBirthSky: Show the planets on the day I was born
birthday.showBirthSky@simple: Show the sky on my birthday
birthday.distance: Since you were born, Earth has carried you {distance} kilometres around the Sun, at about {speed, number} km every second. That is {trips, plural, one {# trip} other {# trips}} to the Moon and back.
birthday.distance@simple: Since you were born, you have travelled {distance} kilometres around the Sun – without ever leaving the ground! That is as far as {trips, plural, one {# trip} other {# trips}} to the Moon and back.
birthday.distance@advanced: Since your birth, Earth’s orbital motion has carried you {distance} km around the Sun at a mean {speed, number} km/s: {trips, plural, one {# return trip} other {# return trips}} to the Moon.

years.intro: A year is one trip around the Sun. Your birthday on another planet comes when it is back where it was on the day you were born.
years.intro@simple: A year is one trip around the Sun. Planets far away take much longer, so you are younger there!
years.intro@advanced: A year is the sidereal orbital period: your birthday on a planet is when it returns to the point of its orbit where it was at your birth.
years.age: {age, plural, =0 {not 1 year old yet} one {# year old} other {# years old}}
years.earthAgeThen: {age, plural, one {You will be # on Earth.} other {You will be # on Earth.}}
years.go: {planetId, select, other {Travel to your next birthday on {planet}}}
years.today: {planetId, select, earth {Happy birthday!} other {Happy birthday on {planet}!}}

days.intro: A day lasts from one sunrise to the next. On Mercury a day is longer than a year, so you have had more birthdays there than sunrises!
days.intro@simple: A day lasts from one sunrise to the next. On some planets the Sun rises again after a few hours, on others only after months!
days.intro@advanced: A solar day (sunrise to sunrise) follows from the sidereal rotation and the orbit: 1/solar = 1/sidereal − 1/year. Venus spins backwards, so its Sun rises every 117 Earth days.
days.lived: {count, plural, one {# day lived} other {# days lived}}

weight.intro: Pick a weight on Earth and see what a scale would show on other worlds.
weight.intro@simple: How heavy would you be on other worlds? Move the slider!
weight.noSurfaceNote: * No ground to stand on: this is the pull at the top of the clouds (on the Sun, at its glowing surface).
weight.note: You stay the same everywhere – only the pull of the world changes.
weight.note@simple: You do not get bigger or smaller – the world just pulls on you harder or more gently!
weight.note@advanced: Your mass stays the same everywhere; only gravity’s pull changes, and with it what a scale shows.

motion.stationary: {body} seems to stand still: it is about to turn round.

motion.retrograde@advanced: {body} is in retrograde motion: seen from {observerId, select, other {{observer}}}, its ecliptic longitude decreases by {rate} a day. Ptolemy explained it with epicycles, Copernicus with a moving Earth.

solarWalk.title: If the Sun were {object}…
solarWalk.lead: …Earth would be {earth}, {earthDistance} away. Every size and distance on this page is the real one, shrunk by the same amount to fit a school field. Take the Sun outside and walk it.
solarWalk.lead@simple: …Earth would be as small as {earth} and {earthDistance} away! Take the Sun outside and walk the solar system.
solarWalk.lead@advanced: …Earth would be {earthSize} across and {earthDistance} away. This is a true-scale model at 1 : {ratio}: every size and every distance is shrunk by the same factor. Take the Sun outside and walk it.
solarWalk.open3d: See it in 3D at true scale

solarWalk.summary@simple: The walk to Neptune is {distance} long. It takes about {time}.
solarWalk.summary@advanced: From the Sun to Neptune: {distance}, about {time} at a walking pace of 4 km/h.

solarWalk.sunStop@advanced: Here the Sun is {object}, {size} across (really {trueSize}). Put it at the start: the school gate or a corner of the field.

solarWalk.star: Now keep going. At this scale the nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is {distance} away – about {flight} by plane. Your whole walk to Neptune fits into that {times} times.
solarWalk.star@simple: And the next star? At this scale it is {distance} away! Even a plane would need about {flight} to get there.
solarWalk.star@advanced: Proxima Centauri, 4.25 light-years away, lands {distance} from the start: {times} times the walk to Neptune, about {flight} of flying at 900 km/h. This small red dwarf would be {size} across, about the size of {thing}.
solarWalk.starLesson: The solar system you just walked is a tiny island in an ocean of empty space.
solarWalk.starLesson@advanced: Between the stars there is almost nothing: the Sun's nearest neighbour is thousands of solar-system walks away.
solarWalk.lineUp: In space the planets are never lined up like this. Each one circles the Sun on its own path, so they are spread out all around it. The walk shows how far each one is from the Sun on average.
solarWalk.lineUp@simple: In real life the planets are never in a row like this. Each one goes round the Sun on its own path.
solarWalk.lineUp@advanced: The planets are never aligned: the walk puts each one at its mean distance from the Sun (the semi-major axis of its orbit). Sizes are mean diameters, from the same data as the 3D model. Proxima Centauri: 4.2465 light-years (Gaia DR3).
solarWalk.tableCaption: If the Sun were {object}: the solar system at 1 : {ratio}
solarWalk.printNote: The circles are printed at their size in the model.
